title: Who Carries the Risk? Capitation, Leases, Reagent Rental and Zero-Based Budgets
summary: Learn how capitation differs from fee-for-service and why it moves cost risk to the laboratory, how finance and operating leases are told apart, why a reagent rental is really a lease, and how a zero-based budget differs from an incremental one.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 13 Hits 5 (capitation, carve-out), 10 (operating vs financial lease) and 11 (zero-based budgeting) and Exam Traps 3 (capitation) and 5 (reagent rental). Capitation and fee-for-service definitions and the risk shift from the Lancet Global Health Commission on financing primary health care, the Cochrane review of payment methods for outpatient facilities and a Kenyan provider-payment study; lease classification from the ASC 842 five criteria as summarized by BerryDunn (the FASB Codification and the IFRS 16 summary page could not be read: the FASB PDF returned 403 and the IAS Plus page rendered no text), with fair-market-value and $1 buyout leases from a 2026 practice-financing review; reagent rental from Accelerate Diagnostics’ 2020 Form 10-K and an online diagnostics discussion study; budgeting from Walsh 2016 and Mitton 2014. The reviewer’s “provider bears all the risk” is qualified (risk-adjusted rates, blended carve-outs; rv-ch13-capitation-risk-blend); the reviewer’s lease definitions (1–3 years, maintenance included, cancellable vs noncancelable) are not the accounting classification criteria (rv-ch13-lease-five-criteria); the reviewer contrasts zero-based with “pro forma” budgets built from history, which the sources call incremental budgeting (rv-ch13-incremental-not-pro-forma). The specific advice to carve out esoteric molecular tests and the Number Vault figures (table) are not taught as fact; the Number Vault table and figure are not mapped. US accounting rules only; Philippine rules not covered.

objectives: Distinguish capitation from fee-for-service and explain who bears the cost risk under each.
Classify an equipment lease as finance or operating using the five classification tests, and explain why a reagent rental is a lease.
Contrast zero-based budgeting with incremental budgeting, including one advantage and one drawback of each.

scenes.title: Three offers on one desk
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: an outpatient laboratory manager has three papers on the desk. (1) A health plan offers a fixed $1.50 per member per month for 2,000 members, covering their routine tests. (2) A vendor offers a “free” analyzer under a reagent rental: the lab only commits to buy the vendor’s reagents for five years. (3) Administration asks for next year’s budget “built from zero.” Question token: “Who carries the risk?”

cues.text: Invented scenario. A health plan offers the lab a fixed payment of one dollar fifty per member per month, for two thousand members.
A vendor offers a free analyzer, if the lab buys its reagents for five years. And next year’s budget must be built from zero.
Three offers, one question: who carries the risk, and what is really being bought?

scenes.title: Paid per test or paid per person
scenes.altText: Two payment cards. Fee-for-service: a payment for each individual service provided, such as a diagnostic test; incentive to provide more services. Capitation: a fixed per-person payment, set and paid in advance, to deliver a defined set of services to each enrolled person for a specified period, whether or not that person seeks care. Risk card: capitation moves financial risk from the payer to the provider; incentives are to control costs and improve efficiency, with the danger of under-providing services or avoiding high-need enrollees.

cues.text: Under fee-for-service, the lab is paid for each individual service it provides, such as each test. More tests mean more payment, which can push toward over-providing.

Under capitation, the provider gets a fixed payment per person, set and paid in advance, to deliver a defined set of services to each enrolled person for a set period, whether or not that person ever needs care.
That moves financial risk from the payer to the provider. If enrollees need more care than the rate assumed, the provider absorbs the cost.
So capitation rewards controlling costs and efficiency, but it can also tempt providers to under-provide care or avoid high-need patients.

scenes.title: Counting the fixed cash, then budgeting from zero
scenes.altText: Worked arithmetic (invented numbers): 2,000 members × $1.50 per member per month = $3,000 per month = $36,000 per year, the same whether the members need 1,000 or 10,000 tests. Carve-out card: blended contracts can pay selected services outside the capitation, fee-for-service. Budget cards: incremental budgeting copies last year’s budget and adds inflation and planned increases (accurate when little changes, but assumes little change); zero-based budgeting starts from scratch each budget cycle, screening every proposed activity and its cost with no assumptions (forces a critical look at everything, but takes much more time).

cues.text: Do the arithmetic. Two thousand members times one dollar fifty per member per month is three thousand dollars a month, or thirty-six thousand a year. That figure does not change if the members need twice as many tests.
That is why contracts can carve selected services out of the capitation and pay them separately, fee-for-service.
Now the budget. Incremental budgeting copies last year’s budget and adds inflation and planned raises. It is accurate when little changes, but it assumes things stay as they were.

Zero-based budgeting starts from scratch each cycle. Every proposed activity and its cost is screened, with no assumptions carried over. It forces a critical look at everything, but it takes much more time.

scenes.title: What the analyzer contract really is
scenes.altText: Lease cards (US GAAP, ASC 842 as summarized by an accounting firm): a lease is a FINANCE lease if it meets ANY of five criteria — ownership transfers by the end of the term; a purchase option the lessee is reasonably certain to exercise; the term covers the major part of the asset’s remaining economic life; the present value of payments equals or exceeds substantially all of the asset’s fair value; the asset is so specialized it has no alternative use to the lessor. Any other lease is an OPERATING lease; both kinds go on the lessee’s balance sheet except certain leases of 12 months or less. A fair-market-value lease works like a long-term rental (return, buy at market value or upgrade at the end); a $1 buyout lease resembles a loan and ends in ownership. Reagent rental card: the customer commits to buy consumables over a stated term at a per-unit price that includes an embedded rental for the instrument; the vendor keeps title and accounts for it as a lease. Hook answer card.

cues.text: Under US accounting rules, a lease is a finance lease if any of five tests is met: ownership transfers, a purchase option the lab will surely use, a term covering most of the asset’s economic life, payments worth substantially all of its fair value, or an asset so specialized nobody else could use it.
Any other lease is an operating lease, which works more like a long-term rental: at the end the lab can return the instrument, buy it at market value, or upgrade.

Reagent rental sounds like renting the instrument, but the lab is really committing to buy reagents for a set term at a price with the instrument rental built in. The vendor keeps title and books it as a lease.
Back to the hook: the health plan shifts risk to the lab, the free analyzer is a lease paid through reagent prices, and a zero-based budget makes every cost earn its place.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Capitation is fee-for-service paid monthly” (✓ fixed payment per enrolled person whatever the services used; risk moves to the provider); “Reagent rental means the instrument is free” (✓ it is an embedded lease: the instrument cost is built into the committed reagent price); “Zero-based budget = last year plus inflation” (✓ that is incremental budgeting; zero-based starts from scratch and screens every cost).

cues.text: Trap one: capitation is just fee-for-service paid monthly. No: it is a fixed payment per enrolled person, whatever services are used, so the risk moves to the provider.
Trap two: reagent rental means the instrument is free. No: it is a lease, paid through a committed reagent price that includes the instrument rental.
Trap three: a zero-based budget is last year plus inflation. No: that is incremental budgeting. Zero-based starts from scratch and screens every cost.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Capitation = fixed payment per enrolled person; risk moves to the provider; carve-outs paid separately”, “Reagent rental = lease inside the reagent price · zero-based budget = justify every cost from scratch”.

cues.text: Capitation pays a fixed amount per enrolled person and moves cost risk to the lab, reagent rental is a lease paid through committed reagent prices, and a zero-based budget makes every cost justify itself from scratch.

props.label: Capitation: fixed per person · risk → provider · carve-outs paid separately
Reagent rental = embedded lease · zero-based = justify every cost

explanation.what: Plain language: under capitation the lab gets a fixed amount for each person enrolled, no matter how many tests they need, so the lab carries the cost if they need more. A lease that is really a purchase on installments is a finance lease; other leases are operating leases. A “reagent rental” is a lease hidden in the reagent price. A zero-based budget starts from nothing each cycle instead of copying last year. Scientific terms: provider payment mechanism, fee-for-service, capitation (per member per month), financial risk, risk adjustment, carve-out, blended payment, lease, finance lease, operating lease, fair-market-value lease, $1 buyout lease, embedded lease, reagent rental, incremental budgeting, zero-based budgeting.
explanation.why: Payment design sets incentives: fee-for-service rewards volume and can lead to over-provision; capitation is paid in advance regardless of use, so it rewards cost control but can lead to under-provision or avoiding high-need enrollees. Lease classification decides whether the lab has effectively bought the instrument with borrowed money. Budget method decides whether old spending is ever questioned.
explanation.measure: Capitation revenue = enrollees × rate per period (invented example: 2,000 × $1.50 per member per month = $36,000 per year). Finance lease if any one of: ownership transfers; reasonably certain purchase option; term is the major part of remaining economic life; present value of payments equals or exceeds substantially all of fair value; specialized asset with no alternative use to the lessor. Otherwise operating. Under ASC 842 both are on the lessee’s balance sheet, except certain leases of 12 months or less.
explanation.differs: Fee-for-service (paid per service, payer bears risk) vs capitation (paid per person in advance, risk shifts to provider); finance lease (purchase financed over time) vs operating lease (rental-like; return, buy at market value or upgrade); reagent rental (instrument cost embedded in committed reagent price) vs outright purchase; incremental (last year plus adjustments) vs zero-based (start from scratch, screen everything).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: identify the payment model from a description, say who bears the risk under capitation, recognize that reagent rental is a lease, classify a lease from its terms, or name the budget that starts from zero.

mnemonic.text: CAPitation CAPS the cash; reagent rental hides the lease in the BOTTLE; zero-based starts on a BLANK PAGE.
mnemonic.explanation: Cap = fixed payment per person whatever is used; bottle = instrument cost inside the reagent price; blank page = no carried-over assumptions.
mnemonic.limitation: Capitation rates can be risk-adjusted and blended with fee-for-service carve-outs, so the cap is not absolute; finance vs operating classification depends on five tests, not on what the contract is called; real budgets often mix methods.

questions.stem: A health plan pays an outpatient laboratory a fixed amount each month for every enrolled member, covering routine testing, regardless of how many tests are ordered. Which statement is correct?

options.text: This is capitation, and the laboratory bears the cost if members need more testing than the rate assumed
options.rationale: Correct. Capitation is a fixed per-person payment made in advance for a defined set of services; it shifts financial risk from the payer to the provider.

options.text: This is fee-for-service, because payment arrives every month
options.rationale: Incorrect. Fee-for-service pays for each individual service; payment frequency does not define it.

options.text: The health plan bears all the cost risk, because it pays in advance
options.rationale: Incorrect. Paying a fixed amount in advance transfers risk to the provider, not the payer.

options.text: Ordering more tests will increase the laboratory’s revenue
options.rationale: Incorrect. Under capitation revenue depends on the number of enrollees and the rate, not on test volume.

questions.stem: A vendor places an analyzer in the laboratory at no up-front charge; the laboratory agrees to buy the vendor’s reagents for five years at a per-test price that covers the instrument. How is this arrangement best described?

options.text: A reagent rental: a lease of the instrument paid through the committed reagent price
options.rationale: Correct. The instrument rental is embedded in the reagent price; the vendor keeps title and accounts for it as a lease.

options.text: A gift of the instrument, since nothing is paid for it directly
options.rationale: Incorrect. The instrument cost is recovered through the reagent price over the committed term.

options.text: An outright purchase, because the laboratory owns the analyzer from day one
options.rationale: Incorrect. The vendor retains title to the instrument.

options.text: Capitation, because the price is fixed per test
options.rationale: Incorrect. Capitation is a payment model for providers per enrolled person, not an equipment contract.

questions.stem: A laboratory director asks every section to justify each activity and its cost for the coming budget cycle, without starting from last year’s figures. Which budgeting approach is this?

options.rationale: Correct. Zero-based budgeting starts from scratch each cycle and screens all proposed activities and expenditures, with no assumptions carried over.
Incorrect. Incremental budgeting starts from last year’s budget and adds inflation and planned increases.
Incorrect. Capitation is a way a payer pays a provider, not an internal budgeting method.
Incorrect. A finance lease is an equipment contract classification, not a budgeting method.

claims.text: Fee-for-service and capitation definitions; capitation paid in advance per enrolled person regardless of use; risk shifts to provider; incentives; carve-outs paid fee-for-service in blended models.
Five finance-lease criteria; other leases operating; balance-sheet treatment; fair-market-value vs $1 buyout leases.
Reagent rental: committed consumable purchase at a price including an embedded instrument rental; vendor retains title; accounted for as a lease.
Incremental vs zero-based budgeting, with advantages and drawbacks.

Reviewer specifics not taught as fact: operating leases last 1–3 years and include maintenance; financial leases are noncancelable and exclude maintenance; esoteric molecular and genetic tests should be carved out of capitation; annual justification in zero-based budgets; “pro forma” budgets; Number Vault capitation figures.
claims.note: Not supported or contradicted by the sources read; see accuracy flags.

claims.text: Scenario and dollar figures invented; cards schematic.

accuracyFlags.issue: The reviewer (Hit 5, Trap 3, 5-Second Recall) says the provider bears all the risk of overruns under capitation. The sources describe capitation as transferring risk to providers, but the Cochrane review says some financial risk is shifted, capitation rates can be risk-adjusted, and blended models pay selected services fee-for-service outside the capitation. The lesson teaches the risk shift without “all”. The reviewer’s advice to carve out esoteric molecular and genetic tests is not taught as fact.

The reviewer (Hit 10) defines an operating lease as 1–3 years with maintenance included and a financial lease as noncancelable, maintenance-free and matching economic life. Under ASC 842 (as summarized by BerryDunn) a lease is a finance lease if any of five criteria is met (ownership transfer, reasonably certain purchase option, major part of remaining economic life, present value substantially all of fair value, specialized asset); term in years, maintenance and cancellability are not the classification tests, and both kinds go on the lessee’s balance sheet. The lesson teaches the five criteria.

The reviewer (Hit 11) contrasts zero-based budgets with “pro forma budgets built from baseline history”. Walsh 2016 calls the history-plus-adjustment method incremental budgeting, and pro forma usually means forecasted financial statements (Mosca 2026). The lesson uses “incremental budgeting”.
Lease classification taught here is US GAAP (ASC 842). Other accounting frameworks and Philippine rules are not covered; MTLE candidates should check local requirements.
